definition.text: Speeding up natural rock weathering by spreading finely ground silicate rock, such as basalt, so it reacts with water and air and removes carbon dioxide.

facts.text: The CO2 ends up stored in solid carbonate minerals or as ocean alkalinity, which also slows ocean acidification.
In nature, rainwater and CO2 form carbonic acid that slowly dissolves minerals; over geological time this helps stabilise Earth's climate.
It could remove 2–4 Gt of CO2 per year.
A 2020 analysis put the cost on cropland at US$80–180 per tonne of CO2, comparable to BECCS and large-scale direct air capture.
Uncertain mineral dissolution rates make its cost and speed uncertain.
Mine tailings and industrial wastes like steel slag can be used first, but more basalt mining might eventually be needed.

definition.text: The proposed gradual reduction of fossil fuel use and production to zero, to cut air pollution, limit climate change and gain energy independence.

facts.text: Fossil fuels cause over 70% of greenhouse gas emissions, so phasing them out is the largest part of limiting warming.
Policies include demand-side measures that cut consumption and supply-side measures that limit production.
Alternatives include electrification, green hydrogen and biofuel.
Most premature deaths from air pollution are due to fossil fuels, and the monetised health benefits of phase-out exceed the cost of the 2 °C goal.
Governments subsidised fossil fuels by about $500 billion a year as of 2019; the IMF's wider definition gave $5.2 trillion in 2017.
As of 2024 global fossil fuel use was still increasing, continuing the trend since 1965.
Workers and politicians tied to fossil fuel industries tend to oppose phase-out unless they have strong alternatives.

title: Phase-out of fossil fuel vehicles
article: Fossil fuel phase-out#Phase-out of fossil fuel vehicles

definition.text: Bans on selling new petrol and diesel vehicles, requiring new cars to be electric or otherwise zero-emission.

facts.text: Many countries have set dates to stop selling petrol and diesel cars, but no timetable exists for ending fossil gas burning.
Many US states have zero-emission vehicle mandates requiring a rising share of electric car sales.

definition.text: Deliberate large-scale intervention in Earth's climate system to counteract human-caused climate change; also called climate engineering.

facts.text: It usually covers two categories: large-scale carbon dioxide removal and solar radiation modification.
Carbon removal is generally counted as mitigation, while SRM reflects some sunlight back to space.
The two differ greatly in mechanisms, timelines and risks and are now usually discussed separately.
A common objection is that focusing on these technologies could undermine efforts to cut emissions.
Effective governance and international oversight are widely seen as essential.

definition.text: Proposed interventions to slow the loss of glaciers, ice sheets and sea ice.

facts.text: They are motivated by fears that feedbacks such as ice-albedo loss could trigger climate tipping points.
Methods include regional sunlight reflection, reflective surfaces, draining water under glaciers and seabed curtains.
The research is early and effectiveness is highly uncertain.

definition.text: The international rules and agreements that address geoengineering, mostly specific to each method.

facts.text: In 2010 the Convention on Biological Diversity set a non-binding framework requiring scientific justification, environmental assessment and oversight.
A 2013 London Protocol amendment created a binding framework for marine geoengineering, starting with ocean fertilization, but it has not entered into force.
